meta.title: Who really said "Religion is regarded by the common people as true, by the wise as false, and by rulers as useful"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Seneca. It's a paraphrase of Edward Gibbon's 1776 line in The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (ch. II). No Seneca text contains it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Religion is regarded by the common people as true, by the wise as false, and by rulers as useful'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Seneca. It's a condensed paraphrase of Edward Gibbon's 1776 sentence in The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, ch. II.

answer.label: Not Seneca — adapted from Edward Gibbon
answer.authorDates: 1737–1794 · English historian, author of The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
answer.sourceLine: This is a loose paraphrase of a famous sentence Edward Gibbon wrote in The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (Vol. I, ch. II, 1776): “The various modes of worship, which prevailed in the Roman world, were all considered by the people, as equally true; by the philosopher, as equally false; and by the magistrate, as equally useful.” No work of Seneca contains this line; the “common people / wise / rulers” wording is a later condensation of Gibbon that drifted onto Seneca’s name.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, Vol. I, ch. II

source.excerpt: The various modes of worship, which prevailed in the Roman world, were all considered by the people, as equally true; by the philosopher, as equally false; and by the magistrate, as equally useful.
trail: Gibbon’s original reads “…considered by the people, as equally true; by the philosopher, as equally false; and by the magistrate, as equally useful” — confirmed in the primary text of Decline and Fall, ch. II.
The Wikiquote Talk investigation concludes the line is Gibbon’s own analysis and that “no verifying record has been found in Seneca’s work.”

The Seneca credit traces to Elbert Hubbard, who in 1904 wrote that Gibbon was “making a free translation from Seneca,” and to Archdeacon F. W. Farrar, who called Gibbon’s passage “little more than a translation from Seneca” — neither pointing to an actual Seneca text, per the same investigation.
An independent write-up at Dead Dog Barking reaches the same verdict: the words are Gibbon’s, and the Seneca attribution is unverified.
source.excerptNote: Gibbon’s actual 1776 sentence. The popular “Religion is regarded by the common people as true…” version is a modern condensation of it, not a quotation of Seneca.

source.rightsNote: The popular wording is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable author, so no rights status can be asserted for it. Its documented source — Edward Gibbon’s sentence in The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (1776) — is long in the public domain, but that is a different set of words from the line credited to Seneca.

author.name: Edward Gibbon
author.heading: About Edward Gibbon
author.metaLine: 1737–1794 · English historian · author of The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
author.bio: Edward Gibbon was an English historian and Member of Parliament whose six-volume History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (1776–1789) is a landmark of Enlightenment scholarship, famous for its irony and its skeptical treatment of religion. The often-misattributed “true / false / useful” epigram is his own summary of Roman religious pluralism in Chapter II, not a translation of any ancient author.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most durable false Seneca quotes. The thought is real, but it belongs to an 18th-century historian, and even his words have been trimmed and rephrased along the way.

items.why: The line is credited to Seneca across countless quote sites, yet no passage in Seneca’s essays, letters, or fragments contains it. The Wikiquote investigation states plainly that “no verifying record has been found in Seneca’s work.”

Gibbon actually wrote of “the various modes of worship… considered by the people, as equally true; by the philosopher, as equally false; and by the magistrate, as equally useful” (Decline and Fall, ch. II). The circulating “religion… common people / wise / rulers” version compresses and reworks that sentence.

Nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century writers muddied the trail: Farrar called Gibbon’s passage “little more than a translation from Seneca,” and Hubbard (1904) repeated that Gibbon was “making a free translation from Seneca” — comments about resemblance, not citations of a real Seneca text, per the Wikiquote Talk record.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea, and the memorable three-part structure, are Edward Gibbon’s from 1776 — not Seneca’s — and the exact popular wording is a later paraphrase of Gibbon, as documented in the Wikiquote investigation.

context.heading: Why the line resonates
lead: Gibbon was describing the religious pluralism of the early Roman Empire, where many cults coexisted. His barbed formulation — that ordinary people believed, philosophers scoffed, and officials found all of it politically convenient — captured a cynical theory of religion’s social function that readers have quoted ever since.

Because Gibbon set the sentence in a chapter about Roman worship, later readers assumed it must be lifted from a Roman author. Seneca, a Stoic who did write skeptically about popular religion, was the natural (if unfounded) candidate.
context.pull: True to the people, false to the philosopher, useful to the magistrate — Gibbon’s verdict on Roman religion, not Seneca’s.
